Title: Rayner to raid interest on tenants’ deposits



The scheme was designed to protect landlords from large unexpected bills, including damages their property may acquire, by storing tenants' deposits in a protected pot when they signed their rental agreements.

Currently, the three providers that run custodial schemes in England - the Tenancy Deposit Protection Service (TDP), the Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS) and MyDeposits - keep the interest earned on tenants' deposits, which pays for a service that is free to landlords and tenants.

The Government could start collecting a portion of the interest as early as March 1 next year. The draft government legislation, which was first seen by The Times, does not specify how much administrators will be required to "pay to the secretary of state".

It confirms that the new rules are designed to try to curb the amount of interest kept by administrators if it "exceeds the amount needed to operate the custodial scheme effectively and provide a reasonable return as profit".

Of the three administrators, the TDS is an independent not-for-profit while the TDP and MyDeposits are private companies.

The plan could bring significant revenue into the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). However, the department said that money raised would be intended "for the benefit of tenants in the private rented sector" through "support[ing] tenant-focused programmes".

According to the Deposit Protection Service (DPS) annual statistical briefing, published March 2025, the DPS held 4.7 million deposits in England and Wales totalling £5.5bn.

Around half of those deposits held by the DPS are custodial deposits which would be subject to the raid, while the other half are insured deposits retained by landlords.

The pot of "custodial" cash is set to increase significantly. Ms Rayner's department is separately proposing to abolish "insured" schemes to prevent landlords from pocketing the interest.

Ms Rayner's department "engaged" with tenant representative groups and some businesses but did not carry out a consultation.

Ministers have confirmed they will publish details of the amount received from the scheme in future at "appropriate intervals". These changes are set to affect tenancies in England alone.

Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, said: "Labour will tax your wages, tax your bills and even want a cut of the interest on your rental deposit. They don't believe that what you earn, or what you own, really belongs to you.

"Even the money that tenants have put aside for their security is no longer safe from this government. This is yet another Labour policy that will push up rents for tenants. It's totally perverse that they pretend to be on the side of tenants while driving up their rents."

An MHCLG spokesman said: "The Tenancy Deposit Schemes do not enable the Government to profit from tenants' deposits.

"These changes will enable more of the interest raised from tenants' deposits to benefit tenants themselves, instead of being kept as profit by the profit companies running the schemes."
